title: RC Low-Pass Filter: Why Gain Rolls Off at the Cutoff
topic: RC low-pass filter — transfer function H(jω) = 1/(1 + jωRC); gain stays flat below the cutoff ω_c = 1/RC and rolls off at −20 dB/decade above; Bode magnitude and phase plots together describe the filter at every frequency

beats.narration: Push a sine wave through an R and a C — what comes out the other side?

elements.content: An R and a C — what frequencies survive?

beats.narration: Here is the filter — a resistor in series, a capacitor to ground, output taken across the capacitor.

elements.content: RC low-pass circuit: V_in on the left, R in series along the top, C to ground at the mid-node, V_out across C

beats.narration: Step the input frequency from low to high. At low frequencies the output tracks the input. As the frequency climbs past the cutoff, the output shrinks and lags behind.

elements.content: Top trace: V_in sinusoid at a stepping frequency
Bottom trace: V_out — same frequency but amplitude scales by 1/sqrt(1+(ωRC)^2) and lags by atan(ωRC)
Live frequency readout: ω = 0.1 ω_c → 10 ω_c

beats.narration: Plot the gain in decibels against frequency on a log axis. Below the cutoff the gain is flat at zero dB; above the cutoff it falls by twenty decibels every decade.

elements.content: Bode magnitude plot — log ω horizontal, |H| in dB vertical
Magnitude curve traces in as a frequency cursor sweeps left to right; flat at 0 dB then rolls off at −20 dB/decade past ω_c
ω_c marker; −3 dB annotation at the corner

beats.narration: Below omega equals one over R C the filter passes the signal through. Above, it kills high frequencies — that is why we call it a low pass filter.

elements.content: low frequencies pass — high frequencies are attenuated
